evidence.description: Comparison with the historical pattern-book approach

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: A grammar reconstructs three shield-back chair designs attributed to Samuel McIntyre and generates new variations on the same Hepplewhite paradigm.

sections.title: Question
sections.text: How can a compact rule system capture recognizable stylistic constraints while allowing variation within them?

sections.title: Premise and claim
sections.text: The shared structure is a compositional paradigm. Creativity can elaborate that paradigm rather than invent a completely new style.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Simplify curved backs into straight-line patterns, generate one symmetric half with parameterized rules and labels, reflect it, then replace lines with curves using a separate procedure.

sections.title: Evidence and examples
sections.text: Figure 22 derives the three starting designs and a new fourth example. Figures 12 and 21 show straight-line alternatives and their curved counterparts.

sections.title: What it establishes
sections.text: The same grammar produces both reconstructions and additional designs under explicit constraints. Knight compares its compactness and usefulness to a pattern book.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: Only one shield-back paradigm is modeled. Seats, legs and carved ornament are excluded; this is a constructive demonstration, not a historical completeness or manufacturing claim.

sections.title: Why read it
sections.text: It makes the distinction between a rule system, its design language and the final interpretation of geometry unusually concrete.

terms.meaning: Rules containing variable dimensions or positions together with conditions on admissible values.
